title: Lviv’s Jewish Suburb Under Attack: Resistance and Loss in 1664
summary: The attack, mass killing, and community defense reveal both the vulnerability and resilience of Jewish life in early modern Lviv.

## A suburb exposed

In 1664, Lviv’s Jews lived in two closely connected quarters: one within the city walls, another outside them. The outer suburb was vulnerable—not only because it lay beyond the gates, but because its residents depended on authorities who could offer protection and fail to provide it. The memorial book’s account places the attack amid years of mounting tension: it describes earlier assaults, anti-Jewish agitation, and Jewish residents preparing to defend themselves. It is the book’s historical narrative, not an independent witness to the events.

The book dates the main assault on the [Jewish suburb](/communities/lviv/records/mention_c2ef8734bc20b5fe22ffc4ee) to 23 May 1664, a Saturday. It says that some 400 armed Jews assembled near the [synagogue](/communities/lviv/records/mention_7ca6d6a4def1252cd8871cd6) and divided into three companies. Their commanders were [Lizer](/communities/lviv/records/mention_6e4fdf92d12affd6dfce6c53), [Kotska](/communities/lviv/records/mention_e93e95dbfd27ea57a33ff47d), and [Tortzin](/communities/lviv/records/mention_24275a927079d9af88ad964a). The defenders repelled two assaults before, according to the book, members of a military unit sent by the authorities joined the attackers. Faced with a larger force, the defenders withdrew. The memorial book reports that assailants entered homes, killed residents, looted property, and desecrated Torah scrolls. The cantor, [Rabbi Shmuel ben Yosef Hayot](/communities/lviv/records/mention_e85ad9589e9237916612da77), was killed while praying.

## What the numbers record—and what they do not

The accounts supplied from the memorial book do not support one simple combined death toll. One event record gives 102 Jewish dead and more than 200 wounded in the May 23 attack. A separate account describes another round of riots on June 12, reporting 129 Jews killed and more than 200 injured, with some wounded dying later. Those figures should not be added together as though they came from a single assault; the book presents distinct episodes. Its later memorial entries also name victims killed outside the city during Iyar, including Azriel Avigdor and Shimon Meir. That excerpt is incomplete, so it cannot establish a full list or a total.

The June account remembers prominent religious and communal figures among the dead. These include [Abraham son of Yosef](/communities/lviv/records/mention_2c960da2a2e72c1b36f69775), [Aharon Yechiel son of Asher](/communities/lviv/records/mention_cadf49f2507c5b77540f4a71), and [Shimshon son of Betzalel](/communities/lviv/records/mention_d51bdd0f68dcbaba8abe05a1). It also names [Yehuda Leib son of Shmuel Katz Margoliot](/communities/lviv/records/mention_a813083ecc5b512f8cf79b0e), described as a leading judge and teacher in Lviv, and [Mordechai son of Yechiel](/communities/lviv/records/mention_b38980d2f75ebd8079b65a1e) and [Shmuel son of Yehuda](/communities/lviv/records/mention_dd660100f62ebc32e7e5dcbf), identified as regional leaders. A separate entry remembers [Shmuel son of Yosef Hayut](/communities/lviv/records/mention_fb07e70b22d2890a757a957a) as a cantor killed while praying in a synagogue abroad; it may relate to the same man as Rabbi Shmuel ben Yosef Hayot, but the excerpts alone do not establish that identification.

The survivors’ losses were not only a matter of numbers. The book names [Rabbi David Halevi](/communities/lviv/records/mention_9e9a7dff5e39b620ed16366c), who escaped into the walled city and lost two sons. It also recalls the killing of 36 “righteous and holy people,” but the passage provided does not make clear whether that figure belongs to the May assault, the later June violence, or a separate memorial context. That uncertainty matters: commemoration preserves names and grief, but its entries do not always map neatly onto a single event.

## Protection requested, protection contested

The memorial book describes Jews asking the authorities for protection before the May attack and preparing to defend themselves when safety seemed uncertain. Afterward, the request became more urgent. It says [Stanisław Potocki](/communities/lviv/records/mention_0a474b9a4e5ad8a142de1929) sent two cavalry companies under Tarnawski after Jewish leaders appealed for help. But the book also recounts how soldiers’ conduct became part of the danger: in its telling, troops joined the attackers in May, while the later arrival of cavalry brought new conflict around the city gates during the June riots. Protection was therefore neither simple nor assured. Military presence could restrain a crowd, yet its deployment and conduct could also intensify disputes.

The account describes a wider failure of security: city officials tried to calm the disorder; some guards or officials would not follow orders; and refugees from the suburb struggled to find shelter inside the walls. The synagogue’s ownership and fate became subjects of dispute in subsequent proceedings. The book also says the authorities investigated the violence, and that a royal order of June 22 called on officials to suppress attacks and punish those responsible. These details come from the memorial book’s account; the independent sources located for this article do not verify its specific figures, named commanders, or proceedings.

## An aftermath without easy closure

The memorial book portrays the aftermath as a struggle over responsibility as well as mourning. It says Jewish leaders reported losses and sought compensation, while city authorities argued over who bore responsibility for failing to protect the community. The book reports that a royal commission found the municipality guilty of negligence and that a 1668 verdict ordered payments to victims’ families and the injured. It also notes that the question remained unresolved in later regional deliberations. The record thus presents a community trying to turn catastrophe into a claim on the law—and encountering delays and contested accountability.

Independent material found in the required archive searches adds context, but not confirmation of this particular seventeenth-century attack. Yad Vashem’s guide to Jewish archival collections in Lviv describes the city as home to one of Eastern Europe’s oldest and most prominent Jewish communities and points readers toward archival holdings for further research. ([collections.yadvashem.org](https://collections.yadvashem.org/en/library/15325230?utm_source=openai)) The USHMM’s Lvov page concerns the city’s much later Holocaust history, not the 1664 riots. ([encyclopedia.ushmm.org](https://encyclopedia.ushmm.org/content/en/article/lvov?utm_source=openai)) No directly relevant YIVO, USHMM, or Yad Vashem account of the 1664 attack appeared in the searches conducted here. That absence is a limit of this research, not evidence that the event did not happen.

What remains in the memorial book is a town’s memory of people who organized to defend one another, survivors seeking refuge, and leaders demanding protection after it had failed. The book’s separate accounts of May and June should remain separate, and its incomplete memorial entries should not be made to say more than they do. Their shared testimony is stark: for Lviv’s Jews, the violence threatened not just lives and homes, but the fragile assurance that the city’s authorities would protect them.
